name: 360 waves / wave brush

card.summary: Brush-and-durag training that coaxes coily hair into ripple patterns; cultural staple, no clinical research.
card.note: Aggressive brushing or tight durags may contribute to traction alopecia (per Grokipedia).

quick.overview:
360 waves are a ripple pattern brushed into short coily hair so it circles the whole head. It is trained with a soft brush, pomade or moisturiser, and a durag.

It grew out of African American barbershop and grooming culture. No clinical studies were found.
quick.mechanism: People brush the hair in circles, keep it moisturised, and compress it with a durag overnight to make it lie flat. Full patterns reportedly take months, and straighter hair often fails to form them.
quick.risks: Aggressive brushing or tight durag use may contribute to traction alopecia, which is generally reversible according to Grokipedia. Claims of balding from waves are described there as unsubstantiated.

lead: Waves are a hairstyle for short, kinky or curly hair in which the curls are brushed or combed flat into a rippling pattern across the scalp.[1] '360 waves' refers to a pattern that encircles the whole head from the crown outward, and variants include 180, 540 and spin waves.[2] The look is built over weeks and months with a short cut, a soft brush, moisturiser or pomade, and a durag or wave cap worn to compress the hair.[1][2]

Wearers use it to get a crisp, uniform, textured finish on a close cut: clearly defined ripples that catch light and read as a deliberate, groomed style, often paired with a sharp lineup. The style is associated with African American men's hair care and barbershop culture and is discussed online on r/360Waves, YouTube and TikTok.[2]

No clinical studies on wave brushing were found. Grokipedia says direct studies of wave-specific routines are limited and that claims waves cause balding are unsubstantiated, while aggressive brushing or tight durag use may contribute to traction alopecia.[2] Wikipedia's description of traction alopecia lists tight headwear among the causes of hairline hair loss.[4]

chain: Short cut plus regular brushing and moisture trains curls to lie flat
A durag compresses the hair and keeps it in place overnight
A defined 360-degree ripple pattern around the head
angle.text: Brushing, moisturising and compressing short coily hair trains the curl pattern into visible waves. Wearers describe the result as a polished, high-definition texture, usually achieved gradually over months.

infobox: Soft boar-bristle brush, pomade, durag or wave cap[1][2]
'Wolfing' (growing out a few weeks) to deepen the pattern[1]

paras: Wikipedia describes waves as a short-cropped cut on top, combined with frequent brushing or combing that trains curls to lie flat; a silky durag or wave cap holds moisture and compresses the hair, and pomades and moisturisers keep the hair from drying out.[1] 'Wolfing' means growing the hair for several weeks to deepen the pattern.[1] Grokipedia gives the general method as cutting hair short, applying moisturiser or pomade, brushing in circles from the crown and compressing overnight with a durag.[2]

In the early 20th century many African American men used texture-altering products, and pomade-and-brush waves became popular; one described method is to wash and brush the hair, apply moisturiser and put on a durag.[1] Grokipedia says brushed waves emerged in the mid-20th century as a low-cost alternative to the lye-based conk, spread through barbershops, and were popularised in 1990s and 2000s hip-hop, with the rapper Nelly often cited; it acknowledges the link to earlier African grooming practices is inferential.[2] The durag itself has a 1960s to 1990s popularisation history.[3]

Grokipedia reports that waves are said to symbolise self-discipline and Black identity, that brushing is said to stimulate the scalp and distribute oils, and that straight or loosely curled hair often fails to form waves, with user-reported failure rates above 50 percent.[2] These figures originate largely in retailer blogs, forums and social media and are not independently verified.[2]

Aggressive brushing or tight durag use may contribute to traction alopecia, generally reversible according to Grokipedia, which says claims that waves cause balding are unsubstantiated.[2] Wikipedia's traction alopecia entry describes hair loss from repeated pulling, lists tight headwear, braids and extensions as causes, and notes that scarring can develop in late stages while early cases are managed by removing the tension.[4]
